title: The Minister's Dilemma

narrative.text: The cabinet room is cold despite the fire — the old heating system in this wing of the palace has been failing since November. Gregor Marić is standing. Colonel Dusek is also standing. They are facing each other across the long table, and the distance between them feels like a border.
They stopped being workers when they occupied the facility.
They occupied it because no one listened.
I'm aware of the sequence of events.

Brief silence. The kind that follows something neither of them can walk back. Both turn when the door opens — Marić with something close to relief, Dusek with the unreadable composure of someone who has not yet decided whether your arrival helps or hinders her position.
Chancellor. The general wants your input.

The cabinet room has not been used for a full cabinet meeting since Halvek's last one in 1961, which was — according to the palace archivist — a forty-minute monologue followed by a vote in which everyone voted the same way. Your cabinet meetings are different. They are arguments. They are supposed to be. Today the argument is between your Labor Minister and your Finance Minister, and it is about to become the argument that defines whether your government can hold its coalition together.

Listen. Unemployment in Kravenstal is twenty-six percent, and in the textile districts it is over thirty — over thirty. These people are not numbers in a ledger. These people are the shift foreman who taught me to pour steel when I was seventeen, the widow on Vostok Avenue who runs a soup kitchen out of her own kitchen because the state closed the community hall, the families in Thornfeld who are making choices between medicine and rent and pretending to their children that everything is fine. I have been a minister for five weeks. Five weeks. In that time I have attended more funerals for people who died of preventable causes than I did in five years of organizing on the factory floor. The government I serve is killing these people — slowly, legally, through budget line items with names like 'efficiency adjustment.' Damn efficiency. I need to know whether this is a temporary phase or the permanent condition of how we govern.

The deficit is not theoretical either. Sixty-five million Krone this year, compounding at 4 percent. If we do not close it, inflation will produce the same outcomes as the budget cuts — at higher velocity, with zero political control over distribution of harm. Gregor is correct about the human cost of 26 percent unemployment. He is incorrect about the alternative. No alternative exists that does not require either spending reduction or monetary expansion. Monetary expansion produces the inflation spiral of 1948 — the one that wiped out private savings and installed Halvek. I am not defending austerity because I prefer it. I am defending it because the numbers leave 0 viable alternatives.

They are both looking at you. Maric with the exhaustion of a man who has been telling hard truths to the people he used to lead and watching their faces as they realize he is now part of the system he once fought. Vostane with the precision of a woman who has run the numbers twelve different ways and found that every path leads through some version of suffering. Vyktor is quiet, which means he has already decided that this is your decision to make and his job is to implement whatever you decide without making it worse.

I put Maric in the cabinet because I wanted the workers to have a voice at the table. I put Vostane in Finance because I needed someone who would tell me the truth about the numbers. They are both doing exactly what I asked them to do and the result is that my government is having an argument with itself in front of me while I try to decide which kind of suffering is less catastrophic. This is what governance is. Not the speeches. Not the votes. The moment when two people you respect disagree about something that will hurt people either way, and you have to choose, and there is no third option that makes everyone whole.

You look at Marić — the man who just spoke of thirty-four families, thirty-four fathers, the widow on Vostok Avenue. He is still breathing hard from the force of his own conviction. You pull a document from your briefing folder. A transfer of ownership from four years ago — Halvek's administration. The Kravenstal Steel Works. Nationalized in 1959.

He stares at the document. The color leaves his face — not in embarrassment, but in the specific shock of a man who has just discovered the floor beneath him is not where he thought it was. A long pause. Then, very quietly:
He sets the document down. His hand is steady but the steadiness costs him something.

I forgot I knew that. The workers I have been organizing for — the ones I have been shouting about for six weeks — they are already state employees. They have been state employees for four years. Under Halvek. Under the government I spent my entire life fighting. He exhales. Not a sigh. Something closer to a surrender. The widow on Vostok Avenue. Her husband died in the Silverbrook collapse. That was 1956. Before nationalization. Before any of this. I have been... I have been shouting the wrong number. For six weeks, I have been shouting the wrong number.

monologue: I put Maric in the cabinet to give workers a voice. I put Vostane in Finance to tell me the truth about the numbers. They're both doing exactly what I asked. The result is my government arguing with itself in front of me while I decide which kind of suffering is less catastrophic. This is governance — not the speeches, not the votes. The moment when two people you respect disagree about something that will hurt people either way, and you have to choose.

choices.text: "Gregor is right. The human cost is too high. Vostane, I need a revised budget framework that spreads the consolidation over five years instead of eighteen months, with a hardship fund for families below the poverty line. Yes, it increases the deficit in the short term. Yes, the IMA will object. The workers of this country did not elect me to manage their immiseration efficiently. They elected me to govern with them, not against them."

reactions.text: He nods once. The kind of nod that is holding something back.
Every day of the occupation costs fourteen thousand Krone.

choices.text: "Vostane is right about the arithmetic. Gregor, I need you to tell the workers what I am going to tell you now: the cuts are not permanent. They are a bridge to solvency. Once the budget is balanced, we redirect resources to social spending — not before. I know that is not what your people want to hear. It is the truth. I will not lie to them about what we can afford just because the truth is painful."

reactions.text: You're making the same mistake they made in '38.
She is already on her radio.
He watches you. Not with judgment. With attention.

choices.text: "Neither of you is wrong, and neither of your solutions works alone. We need growth, not just consolidation. Vostane, redirect twenty million in infrastructure spending to Kravenstal and Thornfeld — public works, housing, rail expansion. Hire locally. Pay union wages. Gregor, I need the Workers' Coalition to sell this to the rank and file: temporary budget discipline paired with job creation that puts money back into the communities the cuts are hurting. If we can show people jobs appearing while the deficit shrinks, we earn the political space to finish the consolidation without losing the country."

reactions.text: Public works. Local hire. Union wages. He counts each word on his fingers like he is checking they are all still there, like someone might take one away. I can sell this. I can take this to Kravenstal tonight and tell them their government sees them. Maybe even believes them. He pauses. Twenty million. That is 20 million more than anyone has spent on the Iron Quarter in my lifetime.

The financial models will require revision. Redirecting 20 million to Kravenstal and Thornfeld shifts the deficit reduction timeline by approximately 6 months. The IMA will note the departure from the consolidation framework. I will prepare the updated projections.
Both camps at the table. That took work.
He glances at the report showing the Kravenstal unemployment figures — twenty-six percent, the same number Marić has been reciting all week. For a moment, he says nothing. Then, almost to himself:
My father worked that mine. Thirty-one years. Died two years after retirement. Lung condition.
He does not elaborate. He does not look at anyone. He moves on to the next item on the agenda.
